answer.label: Not Clayton Christensen — actually Leo McGivena
answer.authorDates: 1896–1980 · New York adman; publicity manager of the Daily News
answer.sourceLine: This exact sentence is not Clayton Christensen’s. It is credited to advertising man Leo McGivena, and its earliest documented printing is Percy H. Whiting’s sales manual The Five Great Rules of Selling (McGraw-Hill, 1947), pages 39–40, which introduces it with the words “Leo McGivena wrote” (Quote Investigator ↗). Christensen’s own drill line was much shorter — “People don’t want to buy a quarter-inch drill. They want a quarter-inch hole!” — and he credited Theodore Levitt, who had himself credited McGivena.

source.excerpt: Leo McGivena wrote: “Last year over one million quarter-inch drills were sold—not because people wanted quarter-inch drills but because they wanted quarter-inch holes. When you buy an automobile you buy transportation. When you buy a mattress you are buying comfortable sleep. When you buy carbon paper you are buying copies.”
trail: 1942 — the idea, before the wording: the earliest strong match Quote Investigator ↗ has found is a Provident Mutual advertisement placed by agent C. C. Wagner in the Somerset American of 12 December 1942, arguing that a million men who bought quarter-inch drills wanted quarter-inch holes. QI adds that it suspects the adage was already in circulation.

1947 — the wording, with McGivena’s name on it: Percy H. Whiting’s The Five Great Rules of Selling ↗ prints the sentence at pages 39–40 and introduces it “Leo McGivena wrote.” This is the earliest documented appearance of the phrasing quoted here.

1969 — Levitt hands it on, correctly: in The Marketing Mode ↗ (McGraw-Hill) Levitt wrote “Leo McGivena once said,” per QI ↗ — he never claimed it, and the Internet Archive record notes the 1974 second edition was retitled Marketing for Business Growth.

2005 — Christensen inherits it: his Harvard Business Review article ↗ with Scott Cook and Taddy Hall used a shorter line and credited Levitt; Wikiquote’s Christensen page ↗ lists no drill-and-hole quotation among his own.
source.excerptNote: As printed in Percy H. Whiting’s sales manual, which is where the wording is first documented. Quote Investigator ↗ reports this passage verified against scans held by the Rubenstein Rare Book Library at Duke University. The version that circulates today usually replaces the dash after “sold” with a comma and drops the three examples that followed.

author.name: Leo McGivena
author.heading: Leo McGivena
author.metaLine: 1896–1980 · New York advertising man; publicity manager of the Daily News
author.bio: Leo McGivena was a New York advertising man who served as publicity manager of the Daily News, then the city’s biggest picture newspaper. Quote researcher Barry Popik gives his dates as 1896–1980 and notes simply that he “worked in advertising”; it is not known when or where he first wrote the drill-and-hole line, only that Percy H. Whiting quoted it under his name in 1947. He is the rare case of a man whose single most-repeated sentence outlived every record of his own career — Theodore Levitt eventually misspelled him “McGinneva” in print.

misattribution.heading: Who really said it
misattribution.intro: This is a misattribution by inheritance. Each famous name in the chain quoted the man before him and said so — and each time the quotation marks got a little looser, until the sentence ended up filed under the most recent celebrity to say it out loud.

items.why: Christensen used a drill-and-hole line, but a different and shorter one, in “Marketing Malpractice: The Cause and the Cure” (Harvard Business Review, December 2005 ↗, with Scott Cook and Taddy Hall), and he introduced it as something Theodore Levitt “used to tell his students” — explicitly not his own (Quote Investigator ↗). The long “Last year over one million…” sentence quoted here is not his at all.

items.scope: The next name up the chain
items.why: Levitt opened The Marketing Mode (1969) with the saying and wrote “Leo McGivena once said” — a credit he repeated in the 1974 edition (QI ↗). Wikiquote ↗ nonetheless carries the short form as a Levitt quotation sourced only to a 2016 Christensen collection — a citation that runs through Christensen rather than back to anything Levitt wrote.

items.scope: How the real name got lost
items.why: By his 1986 Marketing Imagination Levitt was crediting “Leo McGinneva’s famous clarification,” a misspelling recorded by Barry Popik ↗. A name spelled wrong in the standard citation is a name that does not survive being copied.

items.who: Zig Ziglar, and a run of insurance admen
items.why: Zig Ziglar’s 1985 version was its own wording — “Each year over 5 million quarter-inch drills are sold, yet it’s safe to say that nobody wants a quarter-inch drill” — and the idea was already running in life-insurance newspaper advertisements in 1942 and 1946, before any book claimed it (QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the sentence as quoted belongs to adman Leo McGivena, first documented in Percy H. Whiting’s The Five Great Rules of Selling (1947); Christensen wrote a shorter line and credited Levitt, and Levitt credited McGivena (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the line keeps changing hands
lead: The sentence survives because it does a whole marketing lecture in one image: nobody in the hardware aisle actually desires a piece of spinning steel, they desire a hole. The idea is old enough that Quote Investigator ↗ found insurance salesmen already deploying it in newspaper advertisements in 1942 and 1946, before any of the famous names now attached to it had published a word on marketing.

What makes the Christensen credit so sticky is that he genuinely did use a version of the line, at the top of a widely read Harvard Business Review article, and used it brilliantly — as the setup for his argument that firms measure market share of drills rather than of holes. Readers remembered the drill and forgot the footnote. He was quoting Levitt; Levitt was quoting McGivena; McGivena, so far as anyone has documented, was quoting nobody.
context.detailsSummary: Read the full chain of credits
detailsBody: 1942 — the idea, unattributed. An advertisement placed by C. C. Wagner of the Provident Mutual Life Insurance Company in the Somerset American of Somerset, Pennsylvania, is the earliest strong match Quote Investigator has located: hardware stores report a million men bought quarter-inch drills, and not one of them wanted a drill. QI adds that it suspects the adage was already circulating.

1947 — the wording, with a name on it. Percy H. Whiting, who worked for the Dale Carnegie Institute, printed the sentence in The Five Great Rules of Selling and introduced it “Leo McGivena wrote.” This is the first documented appearance of the phrasing people quote today.

1969 and 1974 — Levitt passes it on. Theodore Levitt opened The Marketing Mode with the line and explicitly wrote “Leo McGivena once said.” He repeated the credit in the second edition, retitled Marketing for Business Growth. By his 1986 Marketing Imagination it had degraded to “Leo McGinneva” — a misspelling Barry Popik ↗ records, and a plausible reason the real name dropped out of circulation.

2005 — Christensen inherits it. In “Marketing Malpractice: The Cause and the Cure,” written with Scott Cook and Taddy Hall, Christensen introduced the saying as something Levitt “used to tell his students.” From there it became, in popular retelling, Christensen’s own.
context.pull: Christensen quoted Levitt. Levitt quoted McGivena. Only the drill made it all the way down.

sourcesVerified.claim: Percy H. Whiting's 1947 book The Five Great Rules of Selling (McGraw-Hill), pp. 39-40, prints 'Leo McGivena wrote: "Last year over one million quarter-inch drills were sold—not because people wanted quarter-inch drills but because they wanted quarter-inch holes..."' and identifies McGivena as publicity manager of the New York Daily News; QI reports the 1947 text verified against scans via Duke's Rubenstein Rare Book Library.

The earliest strong match QI found is a 12 December 1942 Provident Mutual advertisement by agent C. C. Wagner in the Somerset American (Somerset, PA); QI conjectures the adage was already in circulation. A 1946 L. E. 'Doc' Hobbs insurance ad follows.

In The Marketing Mode (McGraw-Hill, 1969), ch. 1, p. 1, Theodore Levitt wrote '"Last year 1 million quarter-inch drills were sold," Leo McGivena once said' — i.e. Levitt credited McGivena, not himself.

In the December 2005 Harvard Business Review article 'Marketing Malpractice: The Cause and the Cure', Clayton M. Christensen wrote that Theodore Levitt 'used to tell his students, "People don't want to buy a quarter-inch drill. They want a quarter-inch hole!"' — a shorter wording, credited to Levitt.

Zig Ziglar's 1985 Secrets of Closing the Sale used a different wording: 'Each year over 5 million quarter-inch drills are sold, yet it's safe to say that nobody wants a quarter-inch drill. They want a quarter-inch hole.'

Barry Popik records Leo McGivena's dates as 1896-1980, states he 'worked in advertising' and that it is not known when he first made the saying, quotes the 1947 Whiting page-39 text, and notes Levitt's 1986 Marketing Imagination credits 'Leo McGinneva's famous clarification'.
Barry Popik cites Levitt's Marketing for Business Growth (McGraw-Hill, 1974), p. 8, in which Levitt writes 'Leo McGivena once said' before the drill/hole line.

Wikiquote's Theodore Levitt page carries 'People don't want to buy a quarter-inch drill, they want a quarter-inch hole.' sourced to Clayton Christensen (2016), The Clayton M. Christensen Reader, p. 46 — a citation that runs through Christensen; the page gives Levitt's dates as March 1, 1925 – June 28, 2006.
Wikiquote's Clayton Christensen page contains no quarter-inch drill / quarter-inch hole quotation among his quotes; it gives his dates as April 6, 1952 – January 23, 2020.

The Harvard Business Review article 'Marketing Malpractice: The Cause and the Cure' is by Clayton M. Christensen, Scott Cook and Taddy Hall and is dated December 2005. (Its body text is paywalled; the quoted content is cited to Quote Investigator, not to this page.)
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of The Five Great Rules of Selling by Percy H. Whiting, dated 1947.

The Internet Archive holds Theodore Levitt's 'The marketing mode; pathways to corporate growth', McGraw-Hill, New York, 1969, with a note that a second edition was published in 1974 under the title 'Marketing for business growth'.

Clayton Christensen (April 6, 1952 – January 23, 2020) was the Kim B. Clark Professor of Business Administration at Harvard Business School, developed the theory of disruptive innovation, co-founded the Jobs to Be Done methodology, and wrote The Innovator's Dilemma (1997); the article does not mention the quarter-inch drill saying.
